captions.text: c. 1100 BCE: the kingdom of Anga stands on the middle Ganges.
c. 1100 BCE: the kingdom of Aram-Damascus arises at Damascus.
c. 1100 BCE: the Greek world enters the Dark Age.
c. 1100 BCE: Panchala stands in the Ganges-Yamuna Doab.

12th century BC: Taibo founds Wu in the Yangtze delta (infobox 'Foundation by Taibo: 12th century BC'). The page gives only the century; -1100 is a placeholder for it, and the land is the infobox capital 'modern-day Wuxi and Suzhou, Jiangsu province'.
1100 BCE: the Anau culture ends (infobox "c. 4500 BC - 1100 BC"); no successor is named on the page.
1100 BCE: Neo-Elamite, and three centuries of obscurity.
c. 1100 BCE: the Mycenaean stronghold at Miletus ends.
c. 1100 BCE: the Mycenaean world passes into the Greek Dark Ages.

1080: Herihor is proclaimed first ruling High Priest of Amun, in the nineteenth year of Ramesses XI. The page: "proclaimed as the first ruling High Priest of Amun in 1080 BC"; "He ruled in the south in Thebes, while Ramesses XI ruled from the north in Pi-Ramesses"; the priests were de facto rulers, "writing their names in cartouches and being buried in royal tombs".
1077: Smendes founds the Twenty-first Dynasty at Tanis.
1077: Ramesses XI dies and Smendes founds the Twenty-first Dynasty at Tanis; the priests of Thebes are then the vassal of Tanis in nominal terms only.
c. 1077: Kush goes its own way.
1077: the New Kingdom ends with Ramesses XI; Egypt divides between Tanis and Thebes.
1077: the Theban priests rule the south.
1055 BC: Assyria falls back to its heartland.
1055 BC: the loss of 'most of the empire's territories outside of its heartlands' (Middle Assyrian Empire page).
c. 1050 BCE: the Kingdom of Ammon flourishes at Rabbath Ammon.
c. 1047 BCE: Saul becomes the first king of Israel.
11th century: Shu Zhenduo enfeoffed at Cao.
1046 BC: Eastern Guo begins.
The list row gives '?'
Shang era: Ji is on record before the Zhou.

1046 BC: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffs Zi Yuqi at Ju. Infobox 'Established: 1046 BC'; 'King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed Zi Yuqi at Ju' (footnote citing the Chunqiu Zhengyi); 'a Dongyi state under the Zhou dynasty'.
The list row gives '?'

c. 1046: Lai is already beside the new Qi. The page gives no founding ('Established: ?') and says only that 'As soon as Jiang Ziya, the first ruler of Qi, was enfeoffed at Qi, the state of Lai attacked its capital at Yingqiu'; the Zhou-conquest year is a bridge.
1046 BC: Liu (Lu'an) begins.
11th century BC: Luo is on record.
1046: Pi appears on the page as a Western Zhou neighbour of Song and Tan.
c. 1046: King Wu enfeoffs Duke Tai (Jiang Ziya) at Yingqiu.
c. 1046: King Wu enfeoffs a descendant of Yu the Great at Qi. The page says only 'Established: 11th century BCE' and that King Wu died c. 1043; the Muye year used by other pages is a bridge.
1046 BC: Shu is on record as an ally of King Wu of Zhou at Muye.
1046: the Zhou enfeoff the Shang royal house at Shangqiu and the state of Song begins.
Xia era: Sui is on record before the Zhou.
1046: King Wu founds Tan among the small vassal states after Muye.
1046: the Zhou enfeoff Shu Xiu of Cuo, a brother of King Wu, as viscount of Teng in southern Shandong.
1046: King Wu enfeoffs his uncle Guo Shu.
c. 1046: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffs the rulers of Yan, who rule from Liulihe near Beijing.
The list row gives '?'
1046: the Zhou fief of Yu begins.
1046: King Wu founds the Zhou at Fenghao.
1046: King Wu of Zhou grants Cao Xia the Zhu lands.
c. 1046: King Wu of Zhou wins at Muye; the Shang fall.
1046: the Shang lands after Muye.
1046: Song enfeoffed.
11th century: Cao enfeoffed.
Cliopatria's 750 shape carried back to the enfeoffment, capital Shangqiu

Cliopatria's 750 shape carried back to the enfeoffment, without the State of Ji, which Yan absorbed only 'some time during the 7th century BC'; King Wu 'conferred titles to nobles within his domain, including the rulers of the Yan'; capital Liulihe
'territories centered on the Wei River valley and North China Plain', the royal domain direct and the fengjian states ('he set up the fengjian system') as vassal tint
c. 1045: Cai Shu Du enfeoffed at Shangcai.
1046/45: King Wu enfeoffs Gui Man at Chen.

c. 1045: King Wu enfeoffs the ruler of Ji. In the 11th year of his reign King Wu 'deposed Di Xin and conferred titles to nobles within his domain', including the rulers of Ji and Yan; the page dates it about 1045 BC and calls it 'the first mention of Ji in history'.
c. 1045: Zeng is enfeoffed at Suizhou.
c. 1045: Cai enfeoffed.
1046/45: Chen enfeoffed.
c. 1043 BC: King Wu of Zhou grants Xing to Pengshu.
c. 1042: King Cheng gives Tang to his brother, founding Jin.
c. 1042: Boqin, son of the Duke of Zhou, is enfeoffed at Qufu.
1042 BC: Wu Geng rises at Yin.
c. 1042: the Xu of the Huai River valley first appear in the record, in the Rebellion of the Three Guards against the Duke of Zhou.

capitals.name: Tang, then E, then Jiang (the page lists the capitals in this order without years)

captions.text: 1041 BC: the rebellion at Yin is crushed.
1040 BC: Jiang (Gushi) begins.
1040 BC: Jiang (Zhengyang) begins.
c. 1040: the Zhou enfeoff Kang Shu at Zhaoge and Wey begins on the old Shang heartland north of the Yellow River.
c. 1039: the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign.
c. 1030: Xiong Yi founds Chu at Danyang.
c. 1030: Chu enfeoffed as a viscounty.
